readerTitle: How many subscribers before your software stops losing money?
caseNote: 가상 사례 (회계 사무소가 만든 구독형 도구, 제조사 내부 팀의 딜러용 앱) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 소프트웨어도 고객 한 명마다 드는 비용이 있고, 손익분기점은 그 비용을 뺀 뒤 남는 돈으로 계산해야 한다. 시장이 작으면 판매량보다 가격과 비용 레버가 더 중요하다.
misconception: 소프트웨어는 고객이 늘어도 추가 비용이 거의 없으니 월 고정비를 구독료로 나누면 손익분기점이 나온다.

sources.text: 관리회계의 표준 개념 (손익분기점, 가격·판매량·비용의 세 가지 이익 레버)

cards.title: How many subscribers before your software stops losing money?
body: A small bookkeeping firm built a reporting tool for its own clients. Other firms asked to use it, so the partners turned it into a product: $50 a month per firm.
Software is supposed to cost almost nothing per extra customer. That belief is about to make their target look much closer than it is.

image.label: Bookkeepers at a desk with a laptop showing a subscription counter
image.brief: 작은 회계 사무소 책상. 노트북 화면에 "Paying firms: 120" 카운터와 멀리 있는 깃발 "Break-even?". 서류철과 계산기가 주변에 있음. 실제 소프트웨어 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: How many paying firms to break even?
body: The tool's fixed costs are $12,000 a month: a developer, base hosting and part of a manager's time. Each customer adds $5 in hosting and payment fees. Each also takes about 30 minutes of support a month from staff paid $30 an hour.
How many paying firms does the tool need to cover its costs?

options.feedback: This divides fixed costs by the full $50 price. It treats every dollar as left over, so the target looks easier than it is.
You counted hosting and fees, which is a good start. But support time is also a cost that grows with every customer.
Right. This is the **break-even point**: fixed costs divided by what each customer leaves after all the costs that come with them.

cards.title: Follow one subscriber.
body: Each firm leaves **$30**, not $50. So $12,000 ÷ $30 = 400 firms. The forgotten support time pushed the target up by 133 firms.

cards.title: Software has a shape: big fixed costs, small per-customer costs.
body: Break-even works the same for software as for a bakery. Fixed costs divided by what each sale leaves.

The difference is the shape. Most of a software product's costs are people and tools you pay for every month, no matter how many customers you have. The per-customer costs are small, but people's time often hides inside them.

image.label: Tall fixed-cost block next to thin per-customer slices
image.brief: 왼쪽에 높은 블록 "Fixed costs $12,000 / month", 오른쪽에 얇은 조각들 "$5 hosting", "$15 support". 지원 조각을 사람 아이콘으로 표시해 사람의 시간이 숨어 있다는 점을 강조.

cards.title: Two different moves, the same new target.
body: The partners can pull any of the **three profit levers**: price, volume or cost. Two options cut the target by 100 firms:
list: **Price:** raise it to $60. Each firm leaves $40, so break-even falls to 300.
**Cost:** add help guides so support takes 10 minutes. Support drops to $5, each firm leaves $40, and break-even again falls to 300.
**Volume:** keep everything and sell to 400 firms.
cards.callout: Same result on paper. The real question is which one your customers will accept.

cards.title: Breaking even once isn't the finish line.
body: Subscribers leave. If 10 firms cancel each month, the tool must keep signing new ones just to stay at 400.

Monthly break-even also ignores what was spent building the tool before launch. Covering this month's costs doesn't pay that back. And fixed costs creep up as the product grows: a second developer moves the target too.

cards.title: Now it's a team inside a manufacturer.
body: A four-person team at an equipment maker sells a maintenance app to the company's dealers. Fixed costs: $40,000 a month. Price: $200 per dealer, with $40 in per-dealer costs. That's 250 dealers to break even. There are 150 on board, and only 300 dealers exist. The boss wants break-even this year.

options.text: Cut the price to $150 to sign up dealers faster
options.feedback: Each dealer would leave $110, pushing break-even to 364. That's more dealers than exist. The price lever moved the wrong way.

options.text: Push sales hard to sign 100 more dealers
options.feedback: The volume lever can work, but it needs 83% of all dealers. With a capped market, volume alone is a fragile plan.

options.text: Add the feature dealers keep asking for and charge $250
options.feedback: Each dealer now leaves $210, so break-even falls to 191. When the market is small, price and cost often matter more than volume.

cards.title: Count every cost a customer brings, then pick the lever that fits.
list: **Break-even point:** fixed costs ÷ what each customer leaves
**The three profit levers:** price, volume and cost each move the target
cards.callout: **Try it today:** list every cost that grows with one more customer, including staff time. Recalculate your break-even with it.
